rv.q: “Safe House,” which would seem in form and subject matter a natural successor, is far neater, but so verbally pared back that it gives the audience too little to hold onto.
Formally, Walsh may be stretching himself, but the contents of this new box are familiar and too frequently underwhelming.
Attending Safe House is an immersive, hypnotic experience filled with haunting song, spell-binding spectacle, and an undercurrent of feeling.
It is a show worth seeing if for nothing more than to sample an out-of-the-ordinary theatrical experience.
For all its fascinations, Safe House is too long and insistent; it undermines its considerable impact -- all but destroying it -- with repetition and noise.

However, given the near-relentless drone of composer Anna Mullarkey’s synthpop score set to Walsh’s lyrics– minimal variations on snippets of inner monologue, a kind of emo sprechstimme –audience empathy is apt to drain fast.

The combination of Mullarkey’s wistful music, Gilmore’s achingly vulnerable performance, and Walsh’s command of the production elements builds a striking environment and creates a mood, but little beyond mood.
Safe House remains too scattershot an exercise in style to move us deeply.

cn.t: Walsh's multimedia song cycle features inventive staging but proves exhausting and hollow, with critics finding more melancholy than substance in this one-woman memory play about Irish trauma.

vr.q: I think if you're open to something that requires that level of engagement or you like experimental pieces that demand dissection and interpretation, this is for you.
